results.result: The HLA region is a hotspot for disease associations, comprising 0.3% of the genome but containing 6.4% of significant GWAS SNP associations. Multiple studies have identified associations between HLA class I polymorphisms and various diseases including autoimmune conditions (ankylosing spondylitis with HLA-B*27, Behçet's Disease with HLA-B*51) and infectious diseases (HIV-1 with HLA-B*57 and HLA-B*35Px).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 are well-supported by citations to published literature (MacArthur et al., 2017; Matzaraki et al., 2017; de Menthon et al., 2009; Pereyra et al., 2010; Carrington and O'Brien, 2003; Martin et al., 2007; Carrington et al., 1999; Kiepiela et al., 2004). These claims establish the background context for the study and are based on established prior work in the field.

results.result: HLA class I molecules bind cytosolic peptides (8-11 amino acids) and serve as ligands for multiple immune cell receptors including TCR on CD8+ T cells, KIRs on NK cells, and LILRs on dendritic cells. Peptide-HLA affinity is a significant determinant of CD8+ T cell responses, with 85% of epitopes binding with ≤500 nM affinity, though 50-66% of binding peptides do not elicit responses. Peptide positions P4-8 are most likely to contact the TCR.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C16 are well-supported by multiple citations to established literature (Chen et al., 2000; Müllbacher et al., 1999; Yewdell and Bennink, 1999; Deng et al., 1997; Boggiano et al., 2005; Assarsson et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2004; Hoof et al., 2010; Rudolph et al., 2006; Garboczi et al., 1996; Calis et al., 2012; Hausmann et al., 1999; Calis et al., 2013). These claims establish the biological foundation for the study's methodology.

results.result: KIRs (expressed on NK cells and some T cells) recognize broad HLA class I groupings based on structural motifs (e.g., KIR2DL3 binds C1 group with lysine at position 80). KIR binding shows weak peptide dependence at positions 7-8. CD94:NKG2A binds HLA-E loaded with leader peptides and plays a key role in NK cell education. LILRB1 and LILRB2 (expressed on myeloid cells) bind different HLA allotypes with varying affinity and affect antigen presenting cell activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C26 are well-supported by citations to established literature (Trowsdale, 2001; Moesta et al., 2008; Sim et al., 2017; Fadda et al., 2010; Maenaka et al., 1999a; Maenaka et al., 1999b; Boyington et al., 2000; Braud et al., 1998; López-Botet et al., 2000; Horowitz et al., 2016; Jones et al., 2011; Bashirova et al., 2014). These claims establish the biological foundation for the different receptor-ligand interactions investigated in the study.

results.result: Multiple competing hypotheses exist for HLA-B*57 protection in HIV-1: (1) preferential presentation of conserved Gag p24 epitopes resistant to escape mutations, (2) KIR ligand binding (KIR3DL1 and KIR3DS1), (3) weak LILRB2 binding reducing DC inhibition, and (4) provision of peptides for HLA-E affecting CD94:NKG2A signaling. The association between B*57 and low viral load is widely cited as evidence for CD8+ T cell importance in HIV-1 control.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C32 are well-supported by citations to published literature (Borghans et al., 2007; Kiepiela et al., 2007; Miura et al., 2009; Boppana and Goepfert, 2018; Walker and McMichael, 2012; Flores-Villanueva et al., 2001; O'Brien et al., 2001; Martin et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2002; Pelak et al., 2011; Bashirova et al., 2014; Horowitz et al., 2016; Yunis et al., 2007). These claims establish the motivation for the study by highlighting the ambiguity in interpreting HLA-B*57 associations.

results.result: In HTLV-1 infection, for all four HLA class I alleles studied (A*02:06, A*02:07, C*08:01, B*54:01), TCR.FS was strongly associated with disease risk in the same direction as the index allele. Inclusion of TCR.FS strengthened the index allele effect in every case. None of the other metrics (iKIR.FS, aKIR.FS, LILRB1.S, LILRB2.S) were significant. The authors conclude that protection/susceptibility is best explained by TCR binding properties and is most likely attributable to CD8+ T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 are supported by regression analysis data presented in Table 1. The statistical analysis shows consistent significant associations for TCR.FS across all four alleles with appropriate p-values, while other metrics show no significance. The conclusion that CD8+ T cells are responsible is a reasonable inference from the data, though it remains an inference rather than direct experimental proof.

results.result: In HTLV-1 infection across all alleles, there was a very strong positive correlation (Rs = +0.76, p=5×10⁻⁶) between protection conferred by an allele and protection conferred by alleles with similar TCR binding. In all 29 alleles examined, the direction of protection was consistent (p=4×10⁻⁹). No association was seen for other metrics, though a weak association for iKIR (Rs = 0.6, p=0.07) was observed when restricted to KIR-binding alleles. TCR.FS remained significant (p=0.0006) even in multivariate models including all other metrics.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C42 are supported by correlation and regression analysis data presented in Figure 2 and accompanying text. The statistical tests are appropriate (Spearman correlation, binomial test) with highly significant p-values. The finding that TCR binding properties determine disease risk across all alleles (not just extreme cases) is a novel and important observation. The consistency across 29 alleles provides strong evidence for the conclusion.

results.result: In the HIV-1 cohort studied, HLA-B*35Px was associated with increased viral load (driven entirely by B*53:01) but not progression. HLA-B*57 was associated with low viral load and slow progression. B*53:01 is unusual in having no similar alleles by TCR or KIR metrics (nearest allele only 46% similar). Alleles similar to B*53:01 in LILRB1/LILRB2 binding had no significant impact on clinical outcome, indicating the detrimental effects are independent of LILRB binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48 are supported by analysis of the IAVI cohort data presented in Table 2 and Appendix 3-table 2. The finding that B*53:01 has no similar alleles by TCR/KIR metrics explains the inability to perform similarity analysis for these metrics. The regression analysis showing no association for LILRB metrics is appropriately powered and supports the conclusion that B*53:01's effects are independent of LILRB binding.

results.result: For protective B*57 alleles in HIV-1 infection, alleles with similar aKIR binding to B*57:01, B*57:02, and B*57:03 were significantly protective. Trends for TCR and LILRB2 binding were observed in isolation, but only aKIR.FS retained significance in multivariate analysis. The authors conclude that the main reason for HLA-B*57 protective effect is attributable to activating KIR binding properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 are supported by regression analysis data in Table 2. The multivariate analysis appropriately tests independence of different metrics. The conclusion that aKIR binding is the main protective mechanism is well-supported by the data showing aKIR.FS retains significance while other metrics lose significance in multivariate models. This represents a major finding that challenges the prevailing CD8+ T cell-centric interpretation.

results.result: B*57:01, B*57:02, and B*57:03 contain the Bw4-80I motif and bind KIR3DS1. In the HIV-1 cohort, aKIR.FS was more protective (Coeff = -0.41, p=0.006) than KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I (Coeff = -0.22, p=0.04). In multivariate models, aKIR.FS remained protective while KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I lost significance. Individuals with KIR3DS1 and group I alleles (aKIR.FS >0.6) were strongly protected (Coeff = -0.4, p=0.007), an effect entirely dependent on KIR3DS1 presence. KIR3DS1 with group II or III alleles offered no protection.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58 are supported by regression analysis data and Figure 3. The comparison between aKIR.FS and KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I demonstrates that the fraction shared metric captures clinically relevant variation missed by the binary KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I classification. The identification of three distinct groups with different protective effects despite identical KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I status is a novel finding. Downsampling analysis (Figure 3C) appropriately addresses the concern that differences might be due to sample size.

results.result: In the HIV-1 cohort among KIR3DS1⁻ individuals, B*57:02 and B*57:03 remained significantly protective (Coeff = -0.58, p=0.027; Coeff = -0.39, p=0.019), indicating not all protective effect is attributable to KIR3DS1 ligand binding. Among KIR3DS1⁻ individuals, TCR binding best explained residual protective effect. The authors conclude HLA-B*57 alleles are protective for two reasons: primarily activating KIR binding properties, and secondarily TCR binding properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 are supported by regression analysis data in Appendix 3-table 5. The stratified analysis by KIR3DS1 status is an appropriate approach to dissect independent mechanisms. The finding that B*57 alleles retain protective effects in KIR3DS1⁻ individuals, best explained by TCR binding, provides evidence for dual mechanisms. This represents a sophisticated analysis revealing that different mechanisms operate in different individuals.

results.result: In HIV-1 infection, rank order of intermediate alleles was highly robust and significantly more informative than random (p<10⁻¹⁶). Unlike HTLV-1, no single interaction explained all HLA associations. The only significant correlation was weak (Rs = 0.29, p=0.048) for LILRB2 binding. The authors conclude that different interactions are responsible for protection conferred by different HLA alleles in HIV-1 infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 are supported by statistical analysis in Appendix 2, Appendix 4-figure 2, and Appendix 4-figure 3. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test appropriately assesses robustness of rank order. The finding that no single interaction explains all associations contrasts with HTLV-1 and suggests more complex immunology in HIV-1 infection. The weak LILRB2 correlation with many exceptions supports the conclusion of heterogeneous mechanisms.

results.result: In the HCV cohort, B*57 protective effect was attributable to B*57:02 (with B*57:03 and B*57:05 showing similar trends but not significant due to low numbers). B*57:01 did not appear protective despite large carrier numbers. Unlike HIV-1, there was no evidence that aKIR-binding properties contributed to protection despite adequate power. Instead, protective effect was explained by TCR.FS, indicating CD8+ T cells are most likely responsible. Omitting covariates strengthened TCR.FS findings while aKIR.FS never became significant.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C72 are supported by regression analysis data in Table 3 and Appendix 3-table 6. The finding that aKIR binding does not contribute to B*57 protection in HCV (unlike HIV-1) is well-supported by consistently high p-values and coefficients near zero despite adequate power. The sensitivity analysis omitting covariates strengthens confidence in the TCR.FS finding. This represents an important pathogen-specific difference in mechanism.

results.result: In HCV infection, rank order of intermediate alleles was robust (p<10⁻¹⁶, 93.8% of runs significant). As with HIV-1, no single interaction explained all HLA associations. The strongest positive correlation was for TCR binding (Rs = 0.21, p=0.09), but this was weak and not significant, indicating that while some alleles' protection is attributable to TCR binding, many alleles are better explained by other factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 are supported by statistical analysis in Appendix 2, Appendix 4-figure 2, and Appendix 4-figure 4. The robustness analysis appropriately uses Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. The weak, non-significant correlation for TCR binding contrasts with the strong correlation in HTLV-1, suggesting more heterogeneous mechanisms in HCV. The conclusion that different factors explain protection for different alleles is reasonable given the data.

results.result: The ancestral haplotype AH8.1 (HLA-A*01:01-B*08:01-C*07:01-DRB1*03:01-DQA1*05:01-DQB1*02:01) has been associated with various autoimmune conditions including Crohn's disease. In the Crohn's cohort studied, B*08:01 and C*07:01 (but not A*01:01) were significantly associated with good prognosis. Despite good power, alleles with similar TCR, iKIR, aKIR, LILRB1, or LILRB2 binding to B*08:01 or C*07:01 were not associated with good prognosis. The authors conclude protection is either attributable to other genes in the extended haplotype or B*08:01/C*07:01 confer protection by a mechanism other than immune receptor binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C82 are supported by regression analysis data in Table 4 and Appendix 3-table 7. The finding that none of the similarity metrics show association despite good power is striking and well-documented with very high p-values. In some cases, the direction of association was reversed (nearby alleles detrimental), which strongly argues against receptor binding as the mechanism. The conclusion is appropriately cautious, acknowledging two possibilities. Citations to prior work on AH8.1 and impaired immune activation (Candore et al., 1995; Lio et al., 1995; Egea et al., 1991) support the alternative mechanism hypothesis.

results.result: In HIV-1 infection, all B*57 alleles with high carrier frequency (B*57:01, B*57:02, B*57:03) are protective. However, in HCV infection, B*57:02 and B*57:03 are protective but evidence for B*57:01 protection is less clear. For HIV-1 proteome, all B*57 alleles are very similar (TCR.FS between B*57:02 and B*57:01 is 0.74). For HCV proteome, B*57:01 is more distant from B*57:02 (TCR.FS drops to 0.58, with 10 alleles more similar to B*57:02 than B*57:01). This provides a plausible explanation for why B*57:01 confers similar protection to B*57:02/B*57:03 in HIV-1 but appears less similar in HCV infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C88 are supported by cohort analysis data and TCR.FS calculations for different proteomes. The observation that B*57:01 protection differs between HIV-1 and HCV is supported by the data. The TCR.FS calculations provide a mechanistic explanation for this difference based on proteome-specific peptide binding. This represents an elegant demonstration of how the method can explain pathogen-specific differences in HLA associations. The inference is well-reasoned though remains an inference rather than direct experimental proof.

results.result: For all three viral infections studied, rank order of 'average' alleles was robust. Three observations support the validity of the approach: (1) TCR.FS finds alleles within the same supertype are more similar than between supertypes (p=3×10⁻⁷), (2) for HTLV-1, very strong positive correlation between allele risk and risk of similar alleles by TCR.FS, and (3) in HIV-1, aKIR.FS revealed clinically relevant subtleties within the KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I group, splitting it into 3 groups with decreasing protection.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 are supported by data in Appendix 2, Appendix 4-figures 1-2, Figure 2, and Figure 3. These validation analyses appropriately test whether the metrics capture biologically meaningful features. The supertype analysis (C90) provides face validity. The strong correlation in HTLV-1 (C91) is unlikely to arise by chance. The refinement of KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I classification (C92) demonstrates clinical utility. Together, these provide strong evidence that the method identifies real biological signals.

results.result: The authors provide methodological caveats: the method should not be used in isolation but alongside other evidence. Many problems in classical HLA association studies (linkage disequilibrium, unmeasured confounding, population stratification) are less problematic with these metrics because many alleles contribute to similarity metrics and are unlikely to all be in linkage disequilibrium with the same polymorphism. Nevertheless, linkage disequilibrium and correlations can distort results and should be investigated. The method should be used with care by someone with knowledge of both the biological problem and dataset structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 represent appropriate methodological cautions and recommendations. The reasoning about why linkage disequilibrium is less problematic (C95-C96) is sound - the aggregation across multiple similar alleles provides some protection against confounding. However, the authors appropriately acknowledge that these issues can still distort results (C97). The recommendation for careful use by knowledgeable researchers (C98) is prudent. These caveats demonstrate scientific rigor.

results.result: The study acknowledges limitations: (1) relatively simple KIR binding group definitions not accounting for KIR allele variation or exceptions to C1/C2 and Bw4/Bw6 rules (though these simplistic groupings have proved powerful in other studies), (2) focus on polymorphic, well-characterized receptor-ligand pairs (TCR-HLA:peptide, iKIR-HLA:peptide, aKIR-HLA:peptide, LILRB1-HLA, LILRB2-HLA), (3) CD94:NKG2A-HLA not investigated due to inability to split alleles beyond binary binders/non-binders, (4) atypical HLA effects not studied, and (5) monomorphic receptor-ligand pairs not studied as they cannot explain polymorphic HLA associations.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C106 represent appropriate acknowledgment of study limitations. The KIR limitation (C99) is real but mitigated by citations showing these simple groupings are informative (C100). The scope limitations (C101-C106) are clearly stated and justified. The CD94:NKG2A limitation (C103-C104) is explained by lack of comprehensive binding data. These limitations do not undermine the main findings but appropriately bound the scope of conclusions.

results.result: The authors suggest future applications: the approach could be used alongside GWAS or candidate gene approaches to investigate HLA associations. Lack of association between near alleles and outcome may indicate the identified allele is a passenger or false positive. The approach differs from Raychaudhuri et al.'s amino acid-level fine mapping, which assumed CD8+ T cell responses explain associations. Genetic association studies provide rare opportunities to uncover causal factors in human disease, and knowing causal factors will lead to better understanding of disease pathogenesis and identification of therapeutic targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C113 represent reasonable suggestions for future applications and broader context. The comparison to Raychaudhuri et al. (C109-C111) appropriately positions this work relative to prior approaches. The statements about genetic association studies (C112-C113) are well-established principles. These claims provide appropriate context and suggest reasonable extensions of the work.

results.result: Methods: NetMHCpan v4.0 was used to predict peptide binding with 2% percentile rank threshold. Proteomes used: HTLV-1 subtype from Japan (J02029), HIV-1 Zambian HIV-C subtype (AB254142), HCV subtype 1a (M62321), and 100 random human proteins for Crohn's disease. For small proteomes (<5000 amino acids), results differ depending on proteome choice, but once proteomes become large, exact choice does not impact results.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C121 describe the computational methods used. NetMHCpan v4.0 is an established, validated tool for peptide-HLA binding prediction. The 2% threshold is standard and supported by citations (Nielsen et al., 2007; Jurtz et al., 2017). The proteome choices are appropriate for the cohorts studied. The observation about proteome size effects (C120-C121) is a reasonable inference about the method's properties.

results.result: The HTLV-1 cohort consists of 392 individuals from Kagoshima, Japan (178 asymptomatic carriers, 214 HAM/TSP cases). Well-documented associations exist between HLA-A*02, HLA-C*08, HLA-B*54 and outcome. HLA-A*02 and HLA-C*08 are protective (reduced HAM/TSP risk), while HLA-B*54 is detrimental (increased risk). At 4-digit resolution: A*02:06 and A*02:07 associated with reduced risk, C*08:01 weakly associated with reduced risk, and B*54:01 associated with increased risk.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C129 describe the HTLV-1 cohort and known associations. The cohort description is clear and appropriate. The associations are supported by citations (Jeffery et al., 1999; Jeffery et al., 2000) and by the authors' own analysis (Appendix 3-table 1). The 4-digit resolution analysis appropriately identifies which specific alleles drive the associations.

results.result: Cohort descriptions: IAVI is a prospective cohort of HIV-1 seroconverters from sub-Saharan Africa (N=568 with CD4 data, N=524 with viral load data). HCV cohort consists of four sub-cohorts: ALIVE (N=226), MHCS (N=295), HGDS (N=100), UK cohort (N=161). Crohn's disease cohort consists of 788 poor-prognosis and 1424 good-prognosis cases.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C133 provide cohort descriptions with appropriate citations to original cohort papers. The sample sizes are clearly stated. These are well-characterized cohorts appropriate for the analyses performed. The descriptions provide necessary context for interpreting the results.
